hook.line: Knock a puck around a tabletop rink. A table that floats it on air took the game into arcades worldwide.
hook.say: Let me show you a game where the puck glides like it’s on ice!

ch.say: It began with a home-made board for some kids.
p: Tabletop hockey goes back to 1932, when Donald Munro of Toronto made a game for his children: rod hockey, where you turn rods to move little players. Sold in a department store, it became a hit.
From 1969, engineers at Brunswick in the USA worked on a table that blows air through tiny holes to float the puck. In 1972 it came out as air hockey.

p: An air hockey table is pierced with countless tiny holes; air blowing up through them lifts the puck a hair, so there is almost no friction and it glides on and on.
The striker goes by many names — mallet, paddle, pusher. This game is a small felt rink with no air, and its trick is the edge shot: catch the puck with the rim of a fast mallet.

ch.say: Plenty of tabletop games to hit things in.
